entries.title: Making a fire
entries.summary: Fire climbs from tinder to kindling to sticks to firewood, and needs dry fuel, heat and air at every step. How you arrange it decides whether you get a campfire, a kiln or a charcoal mound.

sections.text: Every piece in a fire has its own temperature. Heated, a piece first steams off its water, then breaks down into burnable gases and charcoal. The gases burn where they meet the air - those are the flames - and whatever air is left over makes the charcoal glow. All that heat warms the next pieces, the thinnest first, so a fire climbs from small fuel to big.
sections.caption: Fuel, heat and air: take any one away and the fire dies.

sections.text: Each fuel needs a certain heat before it catches, and the bigger the piece, the more heat it takes to get it there:
list: [b]Tinder[/b]: straw (catches at about 230 °C) and dry plant fiber. It flares up at once and is gone in moments.
[b]Kindling[/b]: twigs, at about 290 °C.
[b]Sticks[/b], at about 330 °C.
[b]Firewood[/b] and charcoal at about 380 °C; boards, split wood and big limbs at 420 °C; whole logs at 450 °C.

sections.text: Burning tinder on its own just flares and dies, and neither an ember nor a tinder flame can light firewood directly. Lay tinder, then twigs over it, then sticks, then firewood, all close together. Once two or three kilograms of the pile are alight, the pieces keep each other hot and the fire holds itself.

Wet fuel has to steam its water away before it can burn, and it breaks down far more slowly while it is damp. Fresh-cut, green wood smokes and sulks. The twigs and sticks lying under the tree, and the twigs it drops, are dry; season everything else by leaving it out in the sun and wind for a day or two.

A fire burns what the air can reach. In the open it gets plenty, and wind fans it. Earth walls, stones or a pit around it hold the heat in and make it burn hotter, but every opening you close starves it a little. Packed in earth, it barely breathes at all - which is how charcoal is made.

list: The island's first fire has to come from a [b]fire drill[/b].

After that, carry fire: hold a plain stick, look at a burning fire and press [key]RMB[/key] to light it. A burning stick lasts about two in-game hours - under two real minutes. Touch it to dry tinder or kindling by pressing [key]LMB[/key] on the piece.

Feed a fire by holding fuel and pressing [key]RMB[/key] at it. Sticks are the exception - [key]RMB[/key] at a fire lights a stick - so lay sticks on by placing them on the ground right beside the bed.
Anything lying within about half a meter of the fire bed is part of the fire.
Look at a fire to read it: small flames catching in the kindling, a crackling fire, glowing embers, cold ashes.

sections.text: Pour water on it from a vessel with [key]LMB[/key]: each pour boils away, taking heat with it and soaking the fuel. Or simply let it burn down. Once it has been cold for a little while, any piece that charred right through becomes charcoal, half-burnt pieces become charred wood, and barely touched fuel is just fuel again.

Burning returns the wood's carbon to the air, but its minerals stay behind as ash. When the fire is cold, scoop the ash up with empty hands ([key]E[/key]). Ash is fertilizer: work it into the soil. Rain falling on an open ash bed washes it into the ground right there.

sections.warn: Standing in the flames burns you fast, and anything taken hot out of a fire burns your hands. Rain chills an open fire badly; a roof over it keeps it going.

track.text: Tinder: three bundles of fiber (or two of straw)
Kindling: a handful of dry twigs

entries.title: The fire drill
entries.summary: Spin a stick in the notch of a hearth board until friction makes an ember, then tip the ember into tinder. This is how the island's first fire is made.

sections.text: Friction turns effort into heat. Spin a straight stick fast enough in a notch and the wood dust it grinds off gets hotter and hotter, until it smolders into a glowing ember - tiny, fragile, and enough to start everything else.

list: A [b]hearth board[/b]: lay a stick on the ground, hold a blade (or an axe) and hold [key]LMB[/key] on the stick to carve it.
A second straight [b]stick[/b] to spin: the spindle.
[b]Tinder[/b] in your pack: two bundles of straw or three of plant fiber.
Dry kindling and fuel ready nearby: twigs, sticks, firewood.

steps: Choose your fire spot. Put the hearth board down there and lay dry twigs and a few sticks around it, within about half a meter.
Hold a stick and press [key]LMB[/key] on the board ([i]Drill for fire[/i]). Or hold the board, aim at bare ground and press [key]E[/key].
Hold [key]LMB[/key] and sweep the mouse left and right, fast and steady. The Friction heat gauge climbs: first smoke, then hard smoking.
Keep the heat right at the top for a moment longer and an ember forms in the notch.
Press [key]Enter[/key] within thirty seconds. The ember goes into your tinder, and the tinder is set down right where the board was - burning.
Feed it at once: twigs, then sticks, then bigger wood.

list: [b]Too slow[/b]: below about 60% spin, the heat stalls short of an ember. Longer, faster sweeps.
[b]Stopping[/b]: the moment you stop spinning, the board starts to cool.
[b]Out of breath[/b]: with almost no Stamina left you can barely spin. Rest a moment first.
[b]The ember died[/b]: after thirty seconds it's gone, and the board has cooled to a third of its heat. Spin again.
[b]No tinder[/b]: an ember with nothing to catch in is wasted. Have straw or fiber in your pack before you start.

sections.text: The board and the spindle come back to your pack after every fire; each use burns another notch into the board.

sections.tip: Light one fire with the drill, then never let fire go out completely: a burning stick carries it anywhere on the island.

track.text: Carry a spare stick to spin
Carry tinder (three fiber or two straw)

entries.title: Cooking
entries.summary: Roast tubers and mushrooms at the edge of a fire, and simmer grain with water in a fired pot to make porridge. Leave food in too long and it burns to nothing.

sections.text: Food in a fire is just another thing heating up. From about 90 °C it starts to cook, and by 240 °C or so it cooks quickly - and burns just as quickly if you forget it. Cooking doubles what a tuber does for you, and every cooked portion heals you a little.

steps: Get a fire burning well.
Hold a tuber or a mushroom, look at the fire and press [key]RMB[/key]. It is set down at the fire's edge, on your side.
Wait. At a good fire it roasts in roughly half an in-game hour - around half a minute of real time, quicker in a hot fire. Its name changes to Roasted tuber, or Roasted mushroom, when it's done.
Take it out with [key]E[/key]. If the prompt says [i]hot![/i] it will sting your fingers a little - but leave it much longer and it burns.

sections.text: Only tubers and mushrooms roast into something better. Berries, grain seeds and food that is already roasted simply burn.

Food left in the heat keeps on cooking past done. About one and a half times its cooking time again after it has roasted, it burns to a crisp, and all that's left is a little ash and smoke. Food dropped into the middle of the fire burns far faster than food at the edge.

steps: Fill a fired vessel at the pond ([key]E[/key]) and set it down ([key]RMB[/key]).
Hold grain seeds and press [key]LMB[/key] on the pot to put them in, up to four at a time. Each portion takes four seeds and 0.12 liters of water.
Pick the pot up and put it in the fire with [key]RMB[/key].
Once it has simmered at 95 °C or more for about ten in-game minutes, the grain and water turn to porridge: one portion for every four seeds, as far as the water goes.
Take the pot out - careful, it's hot - and hold it to eat with [key]LMB[/key], a portion at a time: 12% Food, a drink of water and a little health.

list: [b]Boiled dry[/b]: a fierce fire boils the water off before the porridge is done. Put in plenty of water.
[b]Cracked pot[/b]: a pot heated very fast in an open fire can crack and spill everything. Cold water on a hot pot cracks it too.
[b]Unfired pots[/b] won't take grain at all.

sections.tip: A pot holds about one seed for every 0.03 liters it can hold, so a big jar cooks several portions at once.

entries.title: Charcoal
entries.summary: Wood heated with too little air to burn turns to charcoal: light, nearly smokeless fuel with twice the heat of wood. Make it in an earth mound - opened too soon, it all burns to ash.

sections.text: Heated wood breaks down into burnable gases and charcoal. In an open fire the air reaches everything: the gases burn, then the charcoal burns too, and you're left with ash. Cover the fire so that only a trickle of air gets in, and there is just enough to burn the gases. Their heat chars the rest of the wood - and the charcoal survives.

steps: Stack a woodpile, packed close: dry firewood, split wood, sticks, charred wood, with tinder and twigs where you will light it.
Light it and let it get going properly. Cover it before it has caught and it never will.

Dig some earth (four liters to a load). Hold a load and hold [key]LMB[/key] on the fire to pack it on: each load covers the part you aim at first, then thickens it. A small pile takes about four loads to seal, a big one eight or more. Looking at it tells you when it is packed with earth.
Hold a stick and press [key]RMB[/key] on the earth to poke a vent. Two vents is a good start; there's room for up to eight.
Watch the smoke and read the mound - see below. The charring takes a few in-game hours.
When the smoke turns thin and blue, close every vent by packing earth over it, and leave the mound to cool.
When it's cold, dig it open with empty hands or a digging tool: each press of [key]E[/key] takes off a load of earth and gives it back to you. Then pick up your charcoal.

list: [b]Thick white steam[/b]: the wood is drying out. Normal at first.
[b]Dense yellow-gray smoke[/b]: the wood is charring. This is the long middle part.
[b]Thin blue smoke[/b]: it's nearly all charcoal. Seal it now.
[b]Roaring, glowing at the gaps[/b]: too much air - it is burning your charcoal. Close a vent.
[b]Barely smoking[/b]: starved of air. Poke another vent.
[b]Still hot[/b]: give it time to cool before you open it.

sections.caption: Air in a trickle makes charcoal; air in plenty makes ash.
list: [b]Opened too soon[/b]: air rushes into the hot mound and the charcoal burns away to ash.
[b]Sealed too early[/b]: smothered, the wood is barely charred.
[b]Gaping holes[/b], or no cover at all: it burns like an open fire, down to ash.

sections.text: Once the mound is cold, every piece that charred right through is charcoal. Pieces only partly charred come out as charred wood: still good fuel, and halfway to charcoal - stack them into your next mound. Slow, cool charring keeps the most: up to about a third of the wood's weight comes out as charcoal, less if the mound ran hot.
Charcoal holds about twice the energy of wood for its weight, barely smokes, and makes a fiercely hot fire - just the thing for firing pottery.

sections.warn: Digging into a mound that is still hot lets the air in. If the prompt says [i]hot![/i], leave it alone.

track.text: Carry a stick for the vents
